name: fold-catamorphism
intent: Replace hand-written recursion over a recursive structure with one traversal owned by a single driver, so that consuming a list, tree or expression means supplying one combining function per case - the algebra - instead of re-deriving the recursion at every call site.
problem: Every consumer of a recursive structure - a sum, a depth, a renderer, a validator, an interpreter - re-derives the same traversal: match on the constructors, recurse into the children, combine the results. The recursion is duplicated and drifts, a new constructor or a missed empty case has to be patched into each consumer, and the traversal order silently becomes part of every consumer's contract instead of a property of the shape.
context: Applies wherever data is defined recursively and read more often than it is built: sequences and cons lists, binary and rose trees, expression and syntax trees, JSON-like documents, configuration trees, workflow definitions, and graphs made finite by a visited set. It pays off when several consumers share one shape (write the traversal once, vary the algebra), when the recursion is deep or the case set is wide enough that hand-written recursion obscures intent, and it is directly available wherever the platform ships a fold for its own collections - the same idea one layer down on any algebraic data type is the catamorphism.
benefits: The recursion is written once and inherited: a consumer supplies the algebra (one function per case, plus the identity for the empty case) and gets a total, correct traversal instead of its own copy of the descent.

Shape changes localise: a new case changes the algebra's input type, and in a language with exhaustive matching the compiler points at every algebra that must handle it, instead of a default branch silently swallowing it.

The two halves are independently testable: the algebra is a pure function of one layer and can be tested on empty, single and nested layers, while the driver's traversal is validated once against a straightforward recursive reference implementation.

Fold laws support equational reasoning: universality and fusion (h . fold g = fold f whenever h . g = f . map h) show when a second fold can be fused into the first pass, which is how pipelines turn into single traversals.

The algebra is the extension point: the same structure folds into different carriers (text, count, validation, a second structure), replacing a subclass-per-operation hierarchy with a function argument at the call site.
Where the platform supports it, folds short-circuit or stream: lazy right folds, try_fold with ControlFlow, yield returning false and parallel reductions make a fold more than a loop with a lambda.
tradeoffs: The algebra must be total over the cases: a consumer that cares about two of six constructors still writes something for the other four, and adding a case breaks every algebra that exists - folds are open to new operations and closed to new cases, the mirror image of Visitor's trade-off.

Traversal direction is easy to get wrong and is rarely checked: foldLeft, foldRight and a parallel reduce differ for non-associative operations, and the most common vocabulary (reduce, inject, Aggregate, Enumerable.Aggregate) is left-associative with no right-fold counterpart at all.

Laziness cuts both ways: a lazy right fold with a non-strict combine short-circuits on long or infinite structures, but the same fold with a strict combine builds a chain of pending calls (stack overflow on a long structure), and a left fold with a lazy accumulator builds thunks instead of reducing (the classic space leak).

A fold is not automatically stack-safe: the recursive form is one frame per layer of the structure, and most of this catalog's languages give no tail-call guarantee, so deep or input-driven data needs an iterative driver, an explicit stack or a trampoline.

Folds consume and cannot stop: a full traversal is the contract, so search-and-stop, effect interleaving and multi-path exploration have to be expressed with escape hatches (try_fold plus ControlFlow, yield returning false) or replaced by a different traversal; a fold also gives each layer only its children's results, never the original children or the ancestors (that is a paramorphism or zygo/visitor concern).

Cost becomes less transparent: intermediate accumulator allocation (immutable carriers, copy-on-write collections, boxing of the carrier) and per-element closure indirection can dominate the real work, which is exactly why reduce(into:), in-place folds and parallel reduce exist - the abstraction has to be measured before it is spread over a hot path.

participants.responsibility: The shape being consumed - list/sequence, tree, expression AST, document node: it fixes the cases and the recursive positions, and therefore the algebra's type; in the recursive-scheme formulation the shape is the base functor whose least fixed point the data type is.

One function per layer: for a list an identity plus a combine of element and folded tail, for a tree one function per constructor taking the folded children; the only place the consumer's logic lives.
Applies the algebra in place of each constructor: it owns the traversal order (left/right), termination, laziness and stack behaviour, and is written once per shape rather than once per consumer.

The type the structure is consumed into - a number, a string, a record, a second structure, a validation result; it is fixed by the algebra's return type and determines whether the fold allocates per step.

The element the accumulation starts from (the monoid unit for a monoid fold): choosing it wrongly corrupts exactly the empty case, and choosing a mutable object breaks sharing under parallel or repeated folds.

use_cases: Aggregating a collection: sums, counts, extrema, string joining, grouping into a map, and the same folds over a stream where the combine is associative.

Evaluating or interpreting an expression tree: one algebra for evaluation, one for pretty-printing, one for constant folding, one for type checking, all reusing the same node type and the same recursion.
Rendering or serialising a document tree to markup, JSON or a diff, folding the children's rendered results into the parent's.

Collecting validation errors with a monoid carrier (a list of failures or an accumulating Validated), so the fold reports every problem instead of the first one - the case where a fold beats an exception-based loop.
Deriving metrics and analyses from a parse tree: node counts, depth, cyclomatic complexity, free variables, dependency sets in a build graph.
Lowering a workflow, state-machine or policy definition into a runnable plan, where each case contributes its own runtime step and the fold assembles the plan.

Building read models and projections from an event stream: an associative combine over the events yields the current state (and licenses the parallel or partitioned variants); the projection is a fold whose combine is applied to each successive event, and the replay is the fold over the entire event history.
Merging layered configuration trees or environment maps where later layers override earlier ones - a fold whose combine is a per-key merge, with the empty layer as the identity.

SQL query building from a list of conditions: fold a list of predicates into a WHERE clause by combining with AND (or OR), using true or false as the identity - each condition contributes its SQL fragment and the fold assembles the complete query string.

Event-sourced aggregate state reconstruction: replay an event stream through a fold whose carrier is the aggregate state and whose combine applies one event to the current state, producing the current state as the final accumulator.

Template rendering where each node type contributes its rendered output and the children's outputs are combined according to the parent's layout rules - a fold over the template AST into an HTML or text string.

Protocol buffer or schema evolution where each version contributes a transformation and the fold applies the sequence of migrations to produce the final schema - the fold carriers the intermediate schema through each migration step.

Kafka Streams rolling aggregation: KGroupedStream.reduce applies a Reducer (aggValue, newValue) to every record for a key, with the state-store value as the running accumulator and the first non-null record initializing it - a fold over an unbounded stream whose combine must stay associative for repartitioned throughput.

Apache Spark distributed fold: RDD.aggregate and aggregateByKey take a zeroValue, a per-partition seqOp and a cross-partition combOp - the same monoid fold evaluated as partial folds per partition then merged, which is why the guide prescribes reduceByKey/aggregateByKey over groupByKey whenever a fold suffices.
avoid_when: The operation is already a builtin or a platform aggregate: sum, min/max, str.join, String.Concat, Iterator::sum and the LINQ aggregates are the monoid cases, and a plain call states the intent more cheaply than any fold spelling.

The traversal must stop early or produce a new structure rather than a value: find/first/any, take_while (or yield returning false) express the stop, and an unfold/anamorphism produces the new shape - a fold is a total consumer.

The structure is shallow and read once: a direct for loop (or a map/collect call) is shorter, faster and easier to debug, especially when the combine is order-sensitive and an inline lambda would hide the direction.

Only one case matters, or the combine depends on depth/position/parent state: a specialised visitor or a recursion that carries context (para/zygo-style) says what it does; a fold sees one layer and only its children's results.

Cases do not share a shape: broadening-first traversal, per-level processing, or mutually recursive types with different carriers need a generic traversal or an explicit worklist, not one algebra per constructor.

The combine is effectful per element with ordering and failure semantics: an explicit loop, a stream pipeline or async iteration makes the effect, its order and its cancellation visible instead of hiding them in a lambda.

The consumer needs access to the original sub-structure at a layer, not just the folded result of each child: use a paramorphism. The fold carrier only receives the children's folded results, never the children themselves.

Multiple interdependent recursive results are needed at a layer: a zygomorphism (where an auxiliary function produces intermediate values reused across the fold) is more natural than threading state through the carrier.
anti_patterns: Calling a loop a fold: wrapping a mutable accumulator in a lambda and mutating captured state inside the so-called algebra, which destroys the function's purity and with it fusion, parallelism and easy testing.

A non-associative combine in a parallel or unordered fold: subtraction, averaging, string concatenation or a map merge over a parallel reduce, where the combine order is unspecified and the result varies without failing.

Re-deriving the traversal in every consumer: five recursive functions over the same AST (evaluate, print, count, check, collect) instead of one fold per algebra, so each new case must be patched into all five.
Folding everything: expressing search, first-match or validation short-circuit as a fold that must visit the whole structure and then encoding stop with a sentinel or an exception.

Recursive folds presented as safe at any depth: folding an unbounded cons list or tree with a non-tail-recursive fold and treating the resulting stack overflow as a language defect instead of choosing a left fold, trampoline or explicit stack.

Accumulating into a shared mutable container from inside the algebra and relying on evaluation order, which works in a serial loop and silently breaks under laziness, reordering or parallel execution.

Choosing a left fold when the intent is a right fold (or vice versa) for a non-associative operation: the two traversals produce different results and the vocabulary usually does not make the direction explicit, so the wrong fold silently produces wrong answers.
design_principles: Separate the traversal from the case logic: the traversal is a property of the shape, the algebra a property of the use, so one is written once and the other varies freely.
Total, well-founded recursion: every case handled and every recursive call on structurally smaller input, so termination is an argument from the structure rather than from a counter.

Higher-order composition over inheritance: operations become values (the algebra) passed to one driver instead of a subclass per operation, which is the functional counterpart of turning behaviour into data.

Laws as design constraints: associativity (required by parallel and streaming folds), the monoid identity (required by the empty case) and fusion (two folds compose into one pass) are obligations a fold's user must satisfy, not properties the platform checks.
Information hiding: a consumer sees one layer at a time and never the traversal machinery, so the shape can change its representation without rewriting the algebras' signatures.
Choose the carrier narrowly: the algebra's return type is the carrier; avoid overloading it with state that belongs in a separate fold or a paramorphism.
best_practices: Fix the case set and write the algebra as a total function over it: let the compiler's exhaustiveness check be the change detector for new cases, and keep a single explicit arm for the genuinely unreachable case.

Prefer the platform's fold and its documented direction over hand-written recursion, and pass the identity explicitly; when the platform ships a monoid specialization (sum, min/max, join), use it instead of a general fold.
Only use a parallel or unordered fold when the combine is associative (plus commutative for unordered execution); state that obligation in a property test or a comment because no compiler checks it.
Test the algebra on single layers and the fold against a straightforward recursive reference on small structures, including the empty and one-layer cases where the identity shows up.

Keep the carrier cheap: choose an in-place or mutable accumulator (reduce(into:), fold with a mutable carrier, std::reduce) for large or hot folds, and measure before the abstraction's per-step allocation is accepted.
Bound the stack: for input-driven depth prefer an iterative fold, an explicit stack or a trampoline, and test with adversarial depth instead of trusting small examples.

Short-circuit with the platform's sanctioned mechanism (try_fold with ControlFlow, yield returning false, a dedicated find/any primitive) rather than throwing out of an algebra or feeding a sentinel through the carrier.

For expression trees and ASTs, model the base functor explicitly so the recursion-scheme cata can be used; in Haskell the recursion-schemes library (Edward Kmett) provides cata, ana, hylo and their generalisations; in Scala the Matryoshka library provides the same for Fix/Mu/Nu; in Rust the karpal-recursion crate implements cata, ana, hylo, para, histo, futu, zygo and chrono for fixed-point types.

Use foldMap (monoid fold) when the algebra produces a monoid value: foldMap is the optimisation of fold_left(mempty, mappend, map(f, xs)) and the platform can fuse the map and fold into a single pass.

For event-sourced projections, express the projection as a fold whose combine is a pure event-application function; this makes the projection testable by feeding it a list of events without any IO or database, and allows rebuild-from-scratch by folding the entire event history.

When writing an algebra for a new recursive type, write the base functor explicitly and test the algebra in isolation on each constructor before combining with the driver; a unit test supplying only Leaf or only Empty catches an incomplete match before the driver is involved.

State associativity and identity obligations explicitly in property-based tests: no compiler enforces that a combine is associative for a parallel fold, and no runtime error reveals a wrong identity; only a property test that varies the element order and the empty case exercises the contract.
sources: Meijer, Fokkinga & Paterson, Functional Programming with Bananas, Lenses, Envelopes and Barbed Wire (FPCA 1991) - introduces the catamorphism ("banana") as the unique homomorphism from the initial algebra of a functor, i.e. the fold for an arbitrary recursive data type, and the laws used to reason about folds.
https://maartenfokkinga.github.io/utwente/mmf91m.pdf

Gibbons, A tutorial on the universality and expressiveness of fold (Journal of Functional Programming 5(3), 1995) - the standard treatment of fold as the canonical total consumer and of the universality/fusion laws.
http://www.cs.nott.ac.uk/~gmh/fold.pdf
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/recursion+scheme
https://jtobin.io/practical-recursion-schemes
https://hackage.haskell.org/package/recursion-schemes/docs/Data-Functor-Foldable.html
Gibbons, Origami: Programming with Folds (JFP 2003) - extends the fold tutorial to a family of complementary schemes (unfold, hylomorphism) and shows how the same structural pattern unifies them.

https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/S0956796815000258 - Unifying structured recursion schemes (2015) surveys the paramorphism, zygomorphism, histomorphism, futumorphism and dynamorphism extensions of catamorphism and their unification via adjoint folds and rs-fcs.

http://ekmett.github.io/reader/2009/recursion-schemes/index.html - A Field Guide to Recursion Schemes (Redux) by Edward Kmett covers catamorphism, paramorphism, zygomorphism, histomorphism, dynamorphism, and their duals (apomorphism, futumorphism, chronomorphism), with practical examples in Haskell.

https://wiki.haskell.org/Fold - HaskellWiki entry on foldr/foldl covering direction semantics, laziness, the relationship to catamorphism for arbitrary algebraic data types, and the importance of foldl' for strict evaluation.

https://wiki.haskell.org/Catamorphisms - HaskellWiki entry covering catamorphism notation (|φ|F), F-algebras, initial algebras, Mendler-style catamorphisms, cata-cancel/cata-refl/cata-fusion laws, and the generalisation to paramorphisms and zygomorphisms via distributive laws.

https://www.schoolofhaskell.com/user/edwardk/recursion-schemes/catamorphisms - School of Haskell catamorphism chapter explaining cata as an F-algebra homomorphism over the initial algebra, with practical examples of evaluating, pretty-printing and transforming recursive types.

https://recursion-schemes-by-example.chrispenner.ca/articles/recursive/basic-catamorphisms - Recursion Schemes By Example (Chris Penner) contrasts catamorphisms with Foldable, shows how cata enables specific traversal orders (in-order tree traversal) that Foldable cannot express, and demonstrates algebras for expression trees.

https://www.sidorenko.me/blog/2026/04/eventium-event-sourcing-library-for-haskell/ - Eventium blog post on event sourcing in Haskell: projections as folds over event streams, process managers, read-model rebuild via fold, and backend-swappable storage.

https://typelevel.org/cats/typeclasses/foldable.html - Cats Foldable documentation covering foldLeft/foldRight semantics, laziness via Eval, foldMap, and the importance of the lazy foldRight for short-circuiting.
https://github.com/precog/matryoshka - Matryoshka: a Scala library for generalised recursion schemes (Fix, Mu, Nu) with cata, ana, hylo and related schemes, integrating with Cats and Scalaz.

https://github.com/gcanti/fp-ts/blob/master/docs/modules/Tree.ts.md - fp-ts Tree fold (catamorphism) documentation: fold<A, B>(f: (a: A, bs: Array<B>) => B): (tree: Tree<A>) => B as the primary catamorphic traversal for Tree, with foldMap for the monoid variant.

https://hightechmind.io/rust/080-catamorphism.html - Functional Rust catamorphism example: implementing cata over a binary tree in Rust with Box-based recursive types, Clone bounds, and &dyn Fn closures, deriving size/sum/height as algebras.

https://www.tweag.io/blog/2025-04-10-rust-recursion-schemes/ - Tweag blog on practical recursion schemes in Rust: JsonValueF base functor, map transformations, and the connection to fold/catamorphism for bottom-up tree traversals.

https://docs.rs/karpal-recursion/latest - karpal-recursion: a Rust crate providing cata, ana, hylo, para, apo, histo, futu, zygo and chrono for Fix<F> with Rc-based Clone, a practical recursion-schemes library for Rust.

https://functional.works-hub.com/learn/catamorphisms-aka-folds-explained-a5524 - Catamorphisms aka Folds Explained (Functional Works): practical walkthrough of catamorphisms in Haskell with foldr/foldl relationship, algebra construction and the F-algebra formulation.

https://japolly.github.io/recursion-schemes-from-the-ground-up/ - Recursion Schemes from the Ground Up (Nicolas Rinaudo): an accessible Scala introduction to catamorphisms via Fix, F-algebras and the cata function, with comparison to manual recursion.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catamorphism - Catamorphism as the canonical homomorphism from an initial algebra to any other algebra, generalizing fold from lists to arbitrary data types.

https://doi.org/10.1007/3540543961_7 - publisher DOI for Meijer, Fokkinga & Paterson, Functional Programming with Bananas, Lenses, Envelopes and Barbed Wire (1991), the origin of the catamorphism/banana calculus.

https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/developer-guide/dsl-api/ - Apache Kafka Streams DSL documentation: KGroupedStream.reduce/KGroupedTable.reduce as rolling per-key folds with an adder (and subtractor for tables), null handling, and first-non-null initialization.

https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html - Apache Spark RDD Programming Guide: aggregate/aggregateByKey/reduceByKey as zeroValue plus seqOp/combOp folds evaluated per partition and merged, with the guidance to prefer them over groupByKey.

http://jackkelly.name/blog/archives/2020-10-16/accidentally-quadratic_hashmaps/ - Accidentally-Quadratic HashMaps: foldMap/fold over HashMap's monoid union degenerates to O(n^2) via repeated unions; a concrete demonstration that a fold's carrier cost is part of its contract.
https://well-typed.com/blog/90/ - Fixing foldl (Well-Typed): the lazy foldl builds a chain of thunks and is effectively broken for strict accumulation; the case for foldl' as the default reduce.

https://blog.jpalardy.com/posts/reduce-is-not-the-answer/ - Reduce is Not the Answer: critique of reaching for reduce/fold as the default accumulator; map, filter and loops often state intent more clearly and folds hide order and short-circuit semantics.
